title: I live in Athens
title_target: Μένω στην Αθήνα — Meh-noh steen Ah-thee-nah
goal: Talk about where you live, what you do, and your daily activities with first-group verbs — and stop saying pronouns you don't actually need.
bekal: build the six forms of verbs ending in -ω
drop the pronoun, because the ending already shows who
ask questions without changing the word order
use the question words πού, τι, πόσο

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — How long have you been here?
dialogs.intro: Nikos and Ana chat while waiting for the bus. Count how many times the pronouns εγώ and εσύ are **not** said even though the meaning is clear — that's the main lesson of this unit.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I live in Pangrati. And you?

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: I live in Athens too, in Kolonaki. What are you doing here?
lines.literal: I-live — also — I — in-the — Athens, in-the — Kolonaki. what — you-do — here?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I'm studying Greek and working a little.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: Oh, nice! Where do you work?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I work in a café, three days a week.
lines.literal: I-work — in — a — café, three — days — the — week.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: And do you study a lot?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I study every day. But I don't always understand.
lines.literal: I-read — every — day. but — not — I-understand — always.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: Your Greek is very good! How long have you been here?
lines.literal: you-speak — very — well! how-much — time — you-stay — here?

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: Slowly, slowly — that's how we all learn.

notes: **The verb ending already shows who's doing it, so the pronoun gets dropped.** *Μένω* already means "I live"; adding εγώ isn't wrong but sounds emphatic. ⚠️ This goes against English habit, where "live" without "I" means nothing. English-speaking beginners usually say εγώ in every sentence for the first two weeks, then stop on their own.
**When is εγώ used?** For contrast or emphasis: *Εγώ μένω στην Αθήνα, αυτός μένει στη Θεσσαλονίκη.* Nikos uses it in the third line — *Μένω **κι εγώ*** — for exactly that: "me too".
**Κι εγώ = "me too".** Και (and) shortens to **κι** before a vowel: κι εγώ, κι εσύ, κι αυτός. This shortening is the norm in speech; saying *και εγώ* sounds like reading an official text.

**Asking a question changes nothing.** *Μένεις στην Αθήνα.* (you live in Athens) and *Μένεις στην Αθήνα;* (do you live in Athens?) differ by one semicolon and a rising tone at the end. ⚠️ No helper like *do / does*, no inversion as in English. This is a big relief that textbooks rarely mention.

**The question word comes first**: **Πού** μένεις; **Τι** κάνεις; **Πόσο** καιρό; ⚠️ Don't confuse **πού** (where, stressed) with **που** (that / who, unstressed). Here the accent really changes the meaning.
**Τι κάνεις; has two lives.** As a greeting it means "how are you"; as a real question it means "what are you doing". Only the situation tells them apart — if you've just met, it's a greeting.

**Σιγά σιγά** (*see-GHAH see-GHAH*, "slowly, slowly") is one of the phrases you'll hear most in Greece, used for learning languages, for work, and for life in general. It's a close cousin of "take it easy" and "one step at a time" — and the doubling does the work of "little by little".
**Ελληνικά means "Greek (the language)" and is a neuter plural.** So are ινδονησιακά, αγγλικά, γαλλικά. To say "in Greek", use **στα ελληνικά**: *Πώς το λένε στα ελληνικά;*

grammars.title: Group A verbs: six endings for hundreds of words
body: This is the largest verb group in Greek. Every verb whose dictionary form ends in an unstressed **-ω** follows this pattern, with no exceptions you need to worry about at A1.
after: Those six endings — **-ω, -εις, -ει, -ουμε, -ετε, -ουν** — work for δουλεύω, διαβάζω, γράφω, καταλαβαίνω, μαθαίνω, θέλω, ξέρω, βλέπω, πίνω, παίρνω, κάνω, and hundreds more. Learn **one** verb until it's fluent, and for the rest you just swap the stem.

⚠️ **The stress doesn't move** in this group: μέν**ω**, μέν**εις**, μέν**ουμε** — all stressed on the same syllable. That's different from the second group (Unit 11), where the stress is always on the ending.
To negate, **δεν** stands right before the verb and never anywhere else: *Δεν καταλαβαίνω.* *Δεν δουλεύω σήμερα.*

grammars.title: Asking questions: three ways, all easy
body: Greek has no question helper at all. All you need is your tone of voice, or a question word at the front.
after: ⚠️ Don't be tempted to translate "do / does" with anything. There's no equivalent, and hunting for one only makes your sentence odd.
The word **ή** (*ee*, "or") is written with an accent so it isn't confused with **η** (the feminine article). Both are pronounced exactly the same.

sections.title: The twenty most common group A verbs

blocks.text: All the verbs below take exactly the same endings as μένω. Cover the second column and try building the "you" and "we" forms yourself.

blocks.title: Adverbs that instantly enrich your sentences
items: **πάντα** (*PAHN-dah*) always · **συχνά** (*see-KHNAH*) often · **μερικές φορές** (*meh-ree-KEHS foh-REHS*) sometimes · **σπάνια** (*SPAH-nee-ah*) rarely · **ποτέ** (*poh-TEH*) never.
⚠️ **ποτέ needs δεν** in front of the verb: *Δεν πίνω ποτέ καφέ το βράδυ.* Greek uses a double negative — literally "I don't drink never" — which standard English forbids but Greek requires.
**κάθε μέρα** every day · **κάθε βδομάδα** every week · **τώρα** now · **σιγά σιγά** slowly, little by little · **γρήγορα** quickly · **πολύ** a lot · **λίγο** a little.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite without the pronoun, because the ending is enough.
Put the words in the right order.
Translate into Greek. Drop the pronoun.

answers: μένω — δουλεύεις — διαβάζει — μαθαίνουμε — καταλαβαίνετε — ξέρουν
Δουλεύω σε μια καφετέρια. — Μένεις στο Παγκράτι. — Μαθαίνουμε ελληνικά. — Δεν καταλαβαίνω. — Διαβάζετε πολύ.
Πού μένεις; — Διαβάζω κάθε μέρα. — Δεν καταλαβαίνω πάντα. — Πόσο καιρό μένεις εδώ; — Έτσι μαθαίνουμε σιγά σιγά.
Μένω στην Αθήνα. — Πού δουλεύεις; — Δεν καταλαβαίνω. — Μαθαίνουμε ελληνικά κάθε μέρα. — Μένω κι εγώ εδώ.
